title: Size the OCR pool for a burst of uploads

blocks.text: The document service reads the text out of every uploaded scan, a few seconds of OCR each. On a normal day three workers keep up. At the end of the month the accountants upload in bursts, and last month the service ran out of memory with forty thousand scans waiting.

The team's decision: three workers normally, and at most six scans waiting for one. When six are already waiting, the service may take on extra workers for the burst, five at most in total. A scan that arrives when all five are busy and six are waiting must not be lost or refused: the upload thread that brought it reads it itself, which slows that uploader down until the burst passes.
Write `create()` in `src/main/java/practice/OcrPool.java`. The class already has the numbers and a `ThreadFactory` that names the threads. About five lines in total.
The tests hand scans to your pool from a thread named `uploader` and read the pool's size and its queue.

cases.says: scans uploaded one after another are all read, on the pool's named threads
with three workers busy, a fourth scan waits instead of starting a fourth worker
once six scans are waiting, further scans bring in extra workers, up to five
a scan that finds five workers busy and six waiting is still read, on the upload thread that brought it

origin.section: A Full Pool Has to Refuse Work: Bound the Queue and Choose Who Pays

concepts: A ThreadPoolExecutor starts core threads first, then queues, and starts threads past the core only when the queue refuses a task; with an unbounded queue the maximum is never used.
A bounded pool hands a task it cannot take to its policy: AbortPolicy throws to the submitter, CallerRunsPolicy runs it on the submitting thread, and the discard policies drop a task silently.
